analysis.one_liner: Bans slaughtering livestock too sick to stand, requiring humane euthanasia instead.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with broad bipartisan backing, never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Agriculture Committee and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill required slaughterhouses, stockyards, and dealers to humanely euthanize any livestock unable to stand and walk on its own. It barred inspectors from passing meat from downed animals into the food supply and labeled it condemned. Animals could still be moved only while unconscious and only if the Agriculture Department tested them for diseases like mad cow disease. It never got a committee hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers gain because meat from animals too sick to walk is banned from the food supply, lowering the risk of diseased meat reaching stores. Meatpacking workers benefit from safer, more orderly handling of sick animals. Downed livestock is also spared prolonged suffering.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Meat consumers, slaughterhouse workers, and livestock

how_it_helps.text: Requires immediate humane euthanasia of nonambulatory livestock at stockyards, markets, slaughterhouses, and dealers.
Prohibits inspectors from passing meat or carcass parts of nonambulatory livestock through inspection and requires the material be marked 'inspected and condemned,' keeping it out of the food supply.
Bars moving nonambulatory livestock while conscious, and requires any moved animal to remain unconscious until death.
Directs the Agriculture Secretary to issue regulations for humane treatment and handling of downed animals within one year.

analysis.who_pays: Meatpackers and slaughterhouses bear the cost of euthanizing downed animals instead of processing and selling their meat. Stockyards and dealers face new handling requirements.

drawbacks.text: Packers lose the resale value of downed animals they previously processed, raising disposal costs.
Some downed livestock may suffer only temporary or treatable conditions, so mandatory euthanasia sacrifices animals that could recover.
The bill allows the Agriculture Department to test downed animals for disease before euthanasia, which some producers view as heavy-handed federal oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and worker-safety gains from keeping sick animals out of the food supply and off the handling floor are large. The cost is confined to packers and dealers who currently profit from downed animals. The main cost concern is the loss of recoverable animals, which is modest compared to the food-safety benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate bill was referred to the Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 25, 2007 by Senator Daniel Akaka with nine original cosponsors including Republicans Ted Stevens and Susan Collins.
Grew to 26 cosponsors: 20 Democrats, 4 Republicans, 1 Independent Democrat, and 1 Independent.
Read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on January 25, 2007.
No further action was recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee report, no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meatpackers and slaughterhouses benefit because the requirement to euthanize downed animals and ban their meat from the food supply never took effect. Consumers and workers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Daniel Akaka
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 25, 2007 with nine original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Sen. Ted Stevens and Sen. Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan backing from the start.

for.name: 26 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, 20 Democrats, 4 Republicans, and 2 Independents.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the entire 110th Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: Of 26 cosponsors, 20 were Democrats, 4 were Republicans, and 2 were Independents, so support crossed party lines, but no member of the Agriculture Committee scheduled the bill.

industries.note: Packers lose the ability to process and sell meat from downed animals and must pay to euthanize them instead. Their interest in continuing the current practice runs against food safety for consumers and safety for their own workers.
Dealers and stockyards face new handling and euthanasia requirements and cannot ship or sell nonambulatory animals for slaughter. They lose the downed-animal trade.
Producers lose some sale value for injured animals but the bill's findings argue humane handling reduces disease spread and improves product quality across the industry.
